synopsis: Adaptive and Bayesian selection uses previous results, a surrogate model and an acquisition rule to choose subsequent tests, distinguishing boundary learning from optimisation for best or worst settings [f14171, f14173, f14174, f14175]. The booklet recommends these methods for efficiently characterising collision-mitigation decision boundaries and places adaptive search in the proposed campaign’s discovery stream [f7280, f7281, f7354]. Multi-objective and safe Bayesian optimisation can reduce expensive HIL or physical evaluations and constrain exploration, but the cited evidence is general engineering methodology rather than off-road braking research [f6974, f6976]. Its efficiency claims depend on the assumed surrogate and acquisition model; surrogate uncertainty can be wrong, and discontinuities and adaptive bias are additional limitations [f7281, f6862, f6978]. Because adaptive sampling deliberately favours interesting regions, its results cannot support naive binomial confidence intervals or population-rate claims: discovery and boundary characterisation must not be treated as rate estimation [f14177, f7282, f14179, f7401].
